title: Create a Website with AI
objective: Building a world-class website today isn't about memorizing web syntax — it's about curation, problem decomposition, and iterative feedback with AI. Learn to direct AI like an architect: precise structural language first, then style, then motion.

steps.title: A few questions first
steps.description: Diagnostic inputs that tune the rest of the lesson: workspace preference, experience with HTML/CSS and JavaScript, and — most importantly — what the student wants to make. That last answer drives the AI showcase and every build in this lesson.

questions.prompt: How do you like to work?
How experienced are you with HTML and CSS?
What do you want to make?
questions.placeholder: A site for your team, your art, a cause, a business idea — anything.

steps.title: Here's what's possible
steps.description: The AI has generated a polished, professional version of the site the student said they want to make. The workspace is read-only — this step is about looking, not editing. Point out what makes it feel professional: clear sections, visual hierarchy, consistent style. Build excitement: by the end of this lesson they'll know how to direct AI to build things like this.
steps.starterPrompt: Generate a genuinely impressive, professional-quality website for what this student said they want to make — the kind of site a design studio would ship. Multiple clearly distinct sections, strong visual hierarchy, a cohesive color palette, thoughtful spacing, and realistic placeholder content that fits their idea. This is a showcase meant to inspire, so aim high.

panels.caption: You can make this yourself — and you don't need to write thousands of lines of HTML and CSS by hand to do it.
Think of yourself as an architect or a product manager, using AI as your junior developer.
Your job isn't to type every line. It's to direct the vision, ask the right questions, and assemble the pieces.

steps.title: Give it a try!
steps.promptPrefill: Build me a website based on my idea.
steps.description: The student's first build. The prompt box is pre-filled with a simple working prompt — they can fire it as-is or tweak it first. The AI already knows their idea from the questionnaire, so even the generic prompt produces something personal. Encourage a second or third prompt to change or add things; the point is to feel the loop: direct, look, direct again.

panels.caption: So — how did the AI do? Probably good, but maybe not exactly what you pictured.
To get precise control, it helps to speak the language of a web developer. Let's learn the words for the parts of a page.

steps.title: Parts of a webpage
steps.description: A five-question vocabulary check on the parts of a webpage. First-attempt performance decides the next step: strong scores go to a layout-prompting challenge, others to a guided layout fix.

questions.prompt: Where do you usually find the footer on a website?
What does a website header usually contain?

options.label: The site name and main navigation
The full text of every page

questions.prompt: What is a navigation bar for?

options.label: Moving between the pages or sections of a site

questions.prompt: The big attention-grabbing area at the top of a homepage is usually called the…
A grid of small boxes, each showing one item with a picture and short text, is usually called a set of…

steps.title: Fix this layout
steps.description: Foundational path. The starter page has a title, a paragraph, a button, and an image all squeezed into one horizontal row. The student's task: fix the layout direction so the title, paragraph, and button stack vertically in one column, with the image in a second column beside them. They can edit the CSS by hand or direct the AI — either way, the layout words from the quiz (column, section, beside) are the tool. Hint at flex-direction and grouping elements if they're stuck.
steps.successCriteria: The title, paragraph, and button are stacked vertically in one column, and the image sits in its own second column beside them — two columns side by side instead of one squeezed row.

starterFiles.index.html:
Adventure Awaits Travel Club

We plan unforgettable trips for people who want to see the world without the stress of planning every detail themselves.

steps.title: Direct the layout
steps.description: Accelerated path. The student writes a layout-only prompt for a fictional brand: Nimbus, a weather app startup. The constraint is the exercise — describe structural geometry only (sections, columns, placement, hierarchy) and deliberately leave out colors and fonts. If their prompt drifts into styling, remind them: structure first, style later.
steps.successCriteria: The generated page contains at least three visually distinct sections (for example a header, a main content area, and a footer).

panels.caption: Great improvements! You just used structure words — sections, columns, headers — to steer the layout.
That's exactly how professionals direct AI: precise language about what goes where. Now let's aim it at your own site.

steps.title: Build your UI shell
steps.description: Now the real project begins. Using what they learned, the student writes their own prompt to generate the UI shell of THEIR site — the one from the questionnaire. Coach them toward a detailed structural prompt: name the sections, say what goes in each, describe the arrangement. How detailed their prompts are decides the next step, but don't tell them they're being evaluated — just coach.

aiJudge.criteria: The student's build prompts describe concrete page structure: they name specific sections (like a header, hero, cards, or footer) and say something about arrangement or content placement. A vague one-liner like 'make me a website' or 'make it better' does not pass.

steps.title: Upgrade your prompts
steps.description: Foundational path. Help the student upgrade vague prompts into precise ones using a word bank: header, hero, section, card, column, grid, navigation, footer, spacing, alignment. Work through their site one piece at a time — take something vague they want ('make it nicer') and rebuild it as a structural instruction ('add a hero section with a large title and a subtitle, then a row of three cards below it'). Each improved prompt gets fired at their real project so they see precision pay off immediately.

steps.title: Polish & motion
steps.description: Accelerated path. The student directs micro-interactions and polish on their own site: make the feature cards scale up slightly on hover, add a glow to the call-to-action button, smooth transitions on links. Push for specificity — 'scale up by 5% on hover' beats 'add some animation'. This is where directing AI feels like real front-end craft.
presetPrompts: Make the cards scale up by 5% when you hover over them, with a smooth transition.
Add a soft glow effect to the main call-to-action button.

steps.title: Finalize your website
steps.description: Free finishing time. The student rounds out their site — more content, refinements, whatever it still needs — prompting the AI, editing by hand, or both. Celebrate what they've built and how they built it: by directing, decomposing, and iterating, not by memorizing syntax.
